Record artifact non-emptiness instead of a byte count (#944)

* Record artifact non-emptiness instead of a byte count

The index recorded the size of every artifact it covers -- files the same batch
of generators had just rewritten -- so it changed on every run and never
settled. The claim that actually has to hold is narrower: an empty file does not
count as generated, which is why the index reads the filesystem rather than
trusting the declaration. A boolean carries that and nothing else.

Third instance of the same shape in this ledger. uncommittedArtifacts counted
the run's own dirty files, bytes measured files the run had just written, and
both looked like data while being noise about the act of measuring.

commits.author: mohammedwessam2007
commits.message:
Build the six computable frontier artifacts, and split what is left from them (#938)

* Build the six computable frontier artifacts, and split what is left from them

Finishes every contract artifact this repository can honestly produce: baselines,
evaluation epoch, mission DAG, resource allocation, frontier checkpoint, final
frontier state. They are one generator because they are one computation read six
ways -- the checkpoint is the DAG plus the baselines, the allocation is the DAG
filtered, the final state is all of it plus the completion law. Six generators
would mean six reads of the same inputs and six chances to disagree about which
head they describe.

The baselines found something on their first run. artifacts/system-readiness.json
records 871 files parsed; the tree parses 2,189. It records 3,683 deterministic
tests with 3 failures; the tree runs over 7,700 with none, and 168 mutations
against 502 registered guards. Every one of those was written down in good faith
at a moment when it was true. What makes them dangerous is that they read
exactly like a measurement taken now.

So a number's provenance travels with the number. LIVE was measured by the run
that produced the artifact; RECORDED was copied from something somebody else
wrote down, and carries its age. A recorded figure with no timestamp is stale
rather than fresh, because currency can never be established for it at all --
defaulting it to fresh would make the least trustworthy figure in the file look
like the best one. Where a live and a recorded value disagree, the disagreement
is listed and neither is edited: overwriting the record destroys the evidence
that it drifted, and averaging them produces a number describing no tree.

The allocator deliberately does not rank by expected value. No economic prior
exists for any of this work and inventing one would dress a guess as arithmetic.
It allocates across missions that are actionable now and lists the rest with what
they wait on, because a dependency is ours to clear and an external blocker is
not -- conflating them turns a waiting list into a to-do list nobody can finish.

The epoch refuses to claim a trend. One epoch is FIRST_EPOCH__NO_COMPARISON_
POSSIBLE and two are CHANGE_MEASURED__TOO_FEW_EPOCHS_FOR_A_TREND, because a
delta between two points is a difference, not a direction.

With those six written, no absent contract artifact is computable any more, so
V7G009 closes on computable work rather than on total absence, and the eleven
that remain move to V7G010 as external. That is the same split already applied
to the deployment gap, and the absence reasons it rests on were classified before
any of these were built.

Also repairs V7G005. It counted commits ahead of main and reported "nothing
stranded" while this very check sat uncommitted in the working tree. Uncommitted
work is stranded in the most literal sense: it exists on one disk and nowhere
else.

11 tests. 6 mutation guards, all killed.

commits.message:
Separate proof debt from rules no guard can settle, and bind claims to heads (#928)

* Separate proof debt from rules no guard can settle, and bind claims to heads

PHASE 3. Both artifacts exist to stop a number meaning less than it looks like.

The doctor's "unguarded external-effect directives" mixed two things. A
prohibition on an external effect can be settled by removing the protection and
watching a test go red. A permission cannot be settled that way by anyone,
because granting latitude has no failure state to catch. Counting them together
produced a review queue that read as a defect list, and reading all 22 by hand
was the only way to tell which was which.

Now it is computed. Of 262 directives: 43 are not dischargeable by code at all,
177 want an ordinary test, 31 want a mutation guard, 11 want an executable
check. The number worth acting on is 14 -- rules code could settle that it has
not. That is a smaller and truer figure than 19 unguarded, and it is the first
one that is actually a work queue.

The obligation kinds are ordered most-demanding-first, because an external-effect
prohibition also matches the weaker INTERNAL_TEST rule and filing it there would
let a test that merely mentions the subject discharge it. A mention is not
enforcement; that distinction is what the whole constitution effort turns on.

The claim-evidence registry asks a different question: this repository asserts
things about itself -- softwareOpen is 1, 490 mutations killed, canonical V9 not
materialized -- and each was true of some tree at some moment. Nothing checked
whether that moment is this one. It has already gone wrong twice here: a
constitution artifact merged claiming 464 anchors against a tree holding 469,
and a readiness artifact described a commit whose source had since changed.

Running it immediately flagged four stale claims from artifacts generated before
the last squash merge. Regenerating cleared them, which is the check working
rather than a coincidence. Evidence with no head reads NOT_HEAD_BOUND rather
than fresh, because a health probe is timed and not committed, and reading it as
exact-head would make an observation from hours ago look like it was taken at
this commit.

One finding from building it: the canonical-V9 claim originally cited the blocker
document, which records one investigation and goes stale by design. It now cites
the gap ledger, which re-runs the materializer at whatever head it reports. A
claim should point at the thing that re-measures it.

Also classifies the remaining absent artifacts. Seventeen absent was not
actionable; the reason each is absent is. Six are COMPUTABLE_NOW -- ordinary
work waiting to be done. Eleven wait on something no amount of writing produces:
repeated observation, elapsed time, external reality, or a lattice runtime that
does not exist. Writing a status file for a runtime that does not exist would be
precisely the confusion the doctrine names. An absence with no reason is now
reported as a defect in the index, which is how the last one was caught.

11 tests. 6 mutation guards, all killed.

* Make claim staleness about source, not about the head moving

My own test caught this one. Comparing a claim's recorded head against current
HEAD is unsatisfiable: committing the artifact changes HEAD, so a registry
generated immediately before a commit is stale the moment it lands. Every commit
would have produced a red gate, and a staleness signal that fires on everything
trains a reader to ignore the word.

The question that actually matters is the one canon-freshness already asks: has
any source the claim depends on changed since it was measured? An artifact
naming the parent commit with nothing but regenerated artifacts after it is
still describing this tree. So the range is diffed and filtered to
src/scripts/config/migrations/tests, and a stale claim now names the files that
falsified it rather than only asserting it is old.

An unreadable commit range is handled separately and is worse than stale: a
recorded head that cannot be found is a claim whose basis has been rewritten or
lives on another branch, and reporting that as "no changes" would be the exact
inversion.

* Turn a real health probe into evidence, and stop the ledger reading complete

Two ends existed and nothing joined them. waitForUberLitHealth probes a running
service and returns a status; the Ubercel doctor reads contract-bound
AUTHENTICATED_HEALTH signals and reports SERVING or NOT_SERVING from them.
Between the two there was nothing -- so a real probe, /api/health returning 200
against the live Render deployment, was written into a handoff document as a
sentence, and the doctor went on reporting UNKNOWN__ONLY_PROVIDER_BADGES.
Prose is not a signal.

That probe is now recorded with its actual provenance: observed at
2026-09-17T16:46:59.098Z by the deployment session that landed 9df093b2, not by
this one. The doctor consequently reports UNKNOWN__EVIDENCE_STALE. That is the
honest answer and the point of the distinction: we knew the service was healthy
at 16:46, and we do not know it now. "We have no way to know" and "we knew, and
the knowledge expired" are different problems, and only the second is waiting on
time.

What the bridge refuses matters as much as what it does. It never probes, so
running it cannot manufacture the evidence it records -- a test replaces global
fetch with a throw to hold that. A 200 from a URL nobody declared is recorded
and binds to nothing. The right URL with the wrong status does not bind either.
An observation with no observer is refused, because a probe with no observer
cannot later be told apart from one this repository invented; an observation
with no readable time is refused, because it could never be aged and so could
never be known stale.

sourceSideComplete: true -- which was false. Nineteen artifacts the contract
names do not exist, and a ledger with no row for them is not a ledger that
found nothing. V7G009 counts them from the index, which reads statSync rather
than intent, so an empty file cannot close it. softwareOpen is 1 again and
sourceSideComplete is false, which is the true state.

* Repair 14 V9 seed parts, and name the one byte-range nobody has

CLAUDE_START_V9.md requires LOSSLESS_VERIFIED and SHA-256 8ad73f53...e55d
before canonical V9 may be treated as canonical. The carrier in this repository
cannot produce it, and this establishes exactly why rather than leaving the next
session to rediscover it.

The materializer reported SEED_ENCODED_PART_MISMATCH:part-0001.xz.b64 and
stopped. That reads as total corruption. It was not. Fifteen of sixteen seed
parts were each exactly one byte short -- a stripped trailing newline -- and
restoring it makes every one of their encoded SHA-256 hashes match the manifest
exactly. Fourteen are repaired here; part 7 had been repaired already in
8daf918a, which is why it alone verified.

Part 16 is different. It is 6,500 bytes where the manifest requires 12,933,
short 4,823 binary bytes of LZMA-compressed V7 content. That is not a checksum
and nothing in this repository can recompute it. Six mechanisms were tested and
all failed with certain outcomes: both sibling carrier branches carry the same
truncation or commit no parts at all; all 36,521 git objects were scanned by
size and none matches V7's 1,916,551 bytes; the alternate Brotli carrier

Read deployment state through Ubercel instead of off a vendor's badge (#919)

* Read deployment state through Ubercel instead of off a vendor's badge

Ubercel already existed, and I misreported it. src/ubercel-deployment-control-plane.mjs
treats VERCEL as one of five replaceable adapter types, refuses any adapter that
declares deploymentAuthority, and carries the law NO_PROVIDER_IS_THE_CONTROL_PLANE.
A session then read a red Vercel commit status and reported it as UberBond's
deployment truth, in a PR comment and twice in a PR body.

The law was enforced at plan time and nowhere at read time, because nothing
answered "what is our deployment state?" at all. Ubercel could compile a plan
and a failover; it could not be asked what was true now. So the only readable
thing was a vendor badge, and that is what got read.

The distinction this adds: a provider badge is a fact about the provider. It
becomes a fact about UberBond only if UberBond serves from it, which is a
question the badge cannot answer about itself. Only a probe bound to the health
contract UberBond declared, or liveness from a runtime UberBond owns, describes
UberBond.

So a red badge alone reports UNKNOWN__ONLY_PROVIDER_BADGES rather than
NOT_SERVING -- a vendor build failing may be a surface we do not serve from --
and a green badge alone reports the same, which is the more dangerous error in
the other direction and the one a passing build invites.

npm run ubercel:doctor, against the signals as actually observed:

  state: UNKNOWN__ONLY_PROVIDER_BADGES
  contract-bound authoritative signals: 0
  provider badges (each establishes nothing about UberBond):
    vercel [VERCEL] serving=false
    vercel-lite-private [VERCEL] serving=false

That is the honest current state. Nothing in this repository collects
contract-bound health evidence yet, and the doctor says so rather than letting
an absence read as health.

The module is wired to a script rather than classified in the reachability
config, for the reason that config gives: a module reachable only from tests is
not reachable.

13 tests. 5 mutation guards, all killed: a badge establishing serving state, an
authenticated probe counting while unbound from the declared contract, stale and
future-dated evidence counting as current, an adapter promoting its own
evidence, and one authenticated not-serving being outvoted by healthy ones.

On the other named layers: uberagents, uberdistribution, ubereconomy, ubermodels,
uberpay and ubervault have no uber-named module, but each has substantial
capability under its existing name -- 21, 8, 16, 10, 14 and 3 modules
respectively. Those are naming gaps, not capability gaps, and creating uber-named
duplicates of agent-mesh-*, distribution-*, economic-*, agent-model-*, billing-*
and secret-* would be the capability sprawl the canon prohibits. Left alone
deliberately.

Make the constitution's precedence real, and say where it runs out (#917)

* Make the constitution's precedence real, and say where it runs out

The compiler's source list carried the comment "Canon files, in precedence
order. NORTH_STAR.md and the precedence file define that order." That was false
twice over: docs/NORTH_STAR_PRECEDENCE.md ranks ten files and exactly one of
them is in the list, and every compiled directive carried priority: 0, so no
order was applied even within it.

Fixing it turned up two facts worth having.

The precedence law cannot settle any conflict between operative rules. It ranks
ten files, nine of which are the terminal North Star layer. The files that
actually bind an agent -- AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, UBERBOND_CANON.md and the
docs/*_CANON.md set -- carry no relative rank anywhere, so 0 of the 9 detected
conflict candidates have an authored answer. One of them is live: the Wallbreaker
canon prohibits evading provider limits while CLAUDE.md permits automatic
failover, and nothing in the repository says which governs.

That is not mine to answer. Ranking one canon file above another decides which
rule wins in a real conflict, which is an amendment, and F003 says founder
sovereignty rules are not autonomously modifiable. So precedenceFor returns
precedenceRank: null with state UNRANKED__NO_AUTHORED_PRECEDENCE -- the old
priority: 0 read as *highest* precedence, which is the opposite of the truth --
and resolveByPrecedence refuses any pair with an unranked side and names the
source that needs a rank. The question is recorded as FD002 in
artifacts/constitution/open-founder-decisions.json with the three options and
the note that ranking the operative canon in the precedence file resolves the
graph with no code change, because the ranks are parsed from that file rather
than transcribed.

The terminal layer's absence is now declared rather than merely true. Those nine
files hold 886 normative sentences and compiling them would take the constitution
from 262 directives to about 1148, nearly all of them arriving as rules awaiting
a guard. NORTH_STAR.md states their status plainly -- "direction and search-space
canon, not implementation proof" -- and a Directive Object asserts
REPOSITORY_TEST_OR_EXECUTABLE_CHECK, so compiling them would make the opposite
claim about all 886 and bury the 48 external-effect rules that bind behaviour
today. TERMINAL_SOURCES names them with that reason, and a test fails if a
ranked file is ever neither compiled nor declared excluded, which is the
silent-drop case the no-amputation law exists to prevent.

Also adds a coverage rollup per source, so "which canon file is least enforced"
is answerable instead of one number spread across nine files. The answer today
is the assimilation canon and UBERBOND_CANON.md, 4 unguarded external-effect
rules each.

9 tests. 5 mutation guards, all killed: an unranked source reporting as a rank,
a conflict settled by inventing an order, two rules from one source ordered
against each other, a duplicate entry hidden by taking the later rank, and the
terminal layer going quietly absent.
